nodes.description: One KCND3 allele carries a missense variant or small in-frame insertion/deletion in the Kv4.3 subunit. Recurrent alleles include an in-frame deletion p.F227del (SCA22, Chinese and French families) and missense changes such as p.T352P (SCA19), p.T377M, p.M373I, p.S390N, p.G345V and p.V338E. The position of the variant does not map cleanly onto a single clinical form, but early-onset neurodevelopmental presentations tend to carry the more disruptive alleles.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in KCND3 cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 22.
evidence.snippet: We identified heterozygous mutations in the voltage-gated potassium channel Kv4.3-encoding gene KCND3: an in-frame 3-nucleotide deletion c.679_681delTTC p.F227del in both the Chinese and French pedigrees, and a missense mutation c.1034G>T p.G345V in the Ashkenazi Jewish family.

evidence.snippet: We detected a T352P mutation in the third extracellular loop of the voltage-gated potassium channel KCND3 that cosegregated with the disease phenotype in our original family.

genetic_context.description: Usually inherited; de novo variants are reported in severe early-onset cases. Most alleles reduce Kv4.3 current and act dominant-negatively on the wild-type subunit; a minority are gain-of-function, so no single functional category covers the allelic series and none is recorded.

meta.association: Heterozygous missense and small in-frame KCND3 variants cause SCA19/22. Most are loss-of-function and dominant-negative; a minority are gain-of-function. De novo variants occur in severe early-onset cases.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in KCND3 cause spinocerebellar ataxia type 22.
evidence.snippet: Our data identify the cause of SCA19/22 in patients of diverse ethnic origins as mutations in KCND3.

evidence.reference_title: First de novo KCND3 mutation causes severe Kv4.3 channel dysfunction leading to early onset cerebellar ataxia, intellectual disability, oral apraxia and epilepsy.
evidence.snippet: We identified a de novo KCND3 mutation causing the most marked change in Kv4.3's channel properties reported so far, which correlated with a severe and unique spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) type 19/22 disease phenotype.

nodes.description: Early-onset motor coordination and balance defects mirroring SCA22 patients, with Purkinje cell degeneration, a minor Purkinje cell loss, cerebellar neuroinflammation, and ER/Golgi retention of the mutant protein with unfolded protein response activation. Knockout mice have no ataxia, identifying F227del as dominant-negative.

nodes.description: Kv4.3 shapes the A-type potassium current that regulates firing of cerebellar Purkinje cells, where the channel is highly expressed. Loss of this current and the dominant negative suppression of wild-type Kv4.3 alter Purkinje cell excitability, which is proposed to drive the subsequent Purkinje cell loss.

nodes.description: Purkinje cells degenerate and are progressively lost. SCA19 autopsy cerebellum showed severe Purkinje cell degeneration with intracellular accumulation and reduced soma levels of Kv4.3, and the F227del knock-in mouse shows degenerated Purkinje cells, a loss of calbindin-positive Purkinje cells and cerebellar neuroinflammation.

evidence.reference_title: A dominant negative Kcnd3 F227del mutation in mice causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 22 (SCA22) by impairing ER and Golgi functioning.
evidence.snippet: The degeneration and a minor loss of Purkinje cells, together with the concurrent presence of neuroinflammation, as well as the previous finding on electrophysiological changes, may all contribute to the development of the SCA22 ataxia phenotype in mice carrying the Kcnd3 F227del mutant protein.

nodes.description: Loss-of-function KCND3 variants reduce the A-type transient outward potassium current. The mutant subunits are retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, are under-glycosylated and short-lived, and when co-expressed with wild-type subunits they suppress the trafficking, surface expression and current of the wild-type channel in a dominant manner. The regulatory subunit KChIP2 can partially rescue membrane localisation of some mutants.
